title: Comparatives and superlatives
objectives: Form common comparative and superlative adjectives.
Compare two items and one item with a group.
Use better and the best accurately.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: We use a comparative adjective to compare two people or things: ‘This bag is lighter than that bag’. We use a superlative adjective to compare one person or thing with a group: ‘This is the lightest bag in the shop’. The group can be stated directly or understood from the conversation.

Adjectives describe qualities such as size, speed and interest. A comparative often comes before than: ‘The blue car is faster than the red car’. A superlative usually comes after the: ‘The blue car is the fastest of the three’. The does not always appear when another determiner is used, as in ‘my best friend’.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: For many short adjectives, add -er for the comparative and -est for the superlative: small, smaller, the smallest. If an adjective ends in e, add -r or -st: large, larger, the largest. In a short adjective ending in a single vowel plus a single consonant, the consonant often doubles: big, bigger, the biggest.

For an adjective ending in consonant plus y, change y to i before the ending: happy, happier, the happiest. For many longer adjectives, use more and most: interesting, more interesting, the most interesting. A dictionary can help with adjectives that allow more than one pattern.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Some forms are irregular. Good becomes better and the best; bad becomes worse and the worst. Far has farther and further, and farthest and furthest; the forms can differ by context. At this level, focus on good and bad and the regular forms in the examples below.

Read the examples as descriptions of real choices. ‘My room is smaller than yours’ compares two rooms. ‘My room is the smallest in the house’ compares it with all the rooms in the stated group. An adjective after be describes the subject: ‘The test is easier than the last one’.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not use more with an -er comparative in standard English: say ‘bigger’, not ‘more bigger’. Do not use most with an -est form: say ‘the tallest’, not ‘the most tallest’. Use than in the common two-item comparison ‘taller than’, not ‘taller that’.

A superlative needs a meaningful comparison group. ‘She is the tallest’ is clear when the listener knows the group, but not every sentence names it. More and most are also used for quantities, which is a different use. Here they form comparisons with adjectives such as interesting.

examples.sentence: This bag is lighter than mine.
That is the smallest room in the house.
examples.note: Smallest compares one room with the rooms in the house.

examples.sentence: The blue book is more interesting than the red one.
examples.note: More forms the comparative of interesting.

examples.sentence: It is the most interesting film in the series.
examples.note: Most forms the superlative of interesting.

examples.sentence: This test is easier than the last one.
examples.note: Easy changes y to i before -er.

examples.sentence: My second result is better than my first.
examples.note: Better is the irregular comparative of good.

examples.sentence: That was the worst meal of the trip.
examples.note: Worst is the irregular superlative of bad.

common_errors.reason: Do not combine more with bigger.

common_errors.incorrect: It is the most tallest building.
common_errors.reason: Do not combine most with tallest.

common_errors.incorrect: My room is smaller that yours.
common_errors.correct: My room is smaller than yours.

summary: Use a comparative to compare two things, often with than.
